sentences.i: Qaḍā Fakān took to riding horses and going out into the open country with her cousin, racing along with him and roaming far afield.
sentences.n: The print writes Qaḍā here with a dotted yāʾ (قضي); it is read Qaḍā. ṣārat with a present verb, “she took to, began to”. ibn ʿamm, “son of the paternal uncle”, the cousin. al-barr, “the open land” outside the town; the print marks the doubled rāʾ of the first al-barr. sāqa bi-, “to ride hard with”, perhaps “to race with him”; wassaʿa fī al-barr, “to go wide in the open land”, to ride far out. Both are spoken usages, and the second reading is a guess.

sentences.t: وَيَتَعَلَّمَانِ الضَّرْبَ بِالسَّيْفِ الطَّعْنَ بِالرُّمْحِ حَتَّى بَلَغَ عُمْرُ كُلٍّ مِنْهُمَا اثْنَتَىْ عَشْرَةَ سَنَةً
sentences.tr: wa-yataʿallamāni al-ḍarba bi-al-sayfi al-ṭaʿna bi-al-rumḥi ḥattā balagha ʿumru kullin minhumā ithnatay ʿashrata sanatan
sentences.l: And the two would learn the striking with the sword, the thrusting with the lance, until the age of each of them reached twelve years.
sentences.i: And the two of them learned to strike with the sword and thrust with the lance, until each of them was twelve years old.
sentences.n: The print has no “and” between al-ḍarb bi-al-sayf and al-ṭaʿn bi-al-rumḥ; a wa- may have dropped out, and the two are read as a list. bi- here is “with”, the weapon used. ithnatay is printed with ى (اثنتى).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْمَلِكَ انْتَهَتْ أَشْغَالُهُ لِلْجِهَادِ وَأَكْمَلَ الْأُهْبَةَ وَالِاسْتِعْدَادَ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-malika intahat ashghāluhu li-al-jihādi wa-akmala al-uhbata wa-al-istiʿdāda
sentences.l: Then the king, his labours for the holy-war came-to-an-end, and he completed the readiness and the preparation.
sentences.i: Then the king's labours for the holy war were done, and he had made all his preparations ready.
sentences.n: inna al-malika intahat ashghāluhu, “the king, his labours ended”: the sentence names the king first and then says what of his was finished, a common turn. uhba, “readiness, equipment”, and istiʿdād, “preparation”, are a pair of near-synonyms.

sentences.t: فَأَحْضَرَ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي عَزَمْتُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ فَأَذْكُرُ لَكَ وَأُرِيدُ اطِّلَاعَكَ عَلَيْهِ فَأَسْرِعْ فِي رَدِّ الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-aḥḍara al-wazīra dandāna wa-qāla lahu iʿlam annī ʿazamtu ʿalā shayʾin fa-adhkuru laka wa-urīdu iṭṭilāʿaka ʿalayhi fa-asriʿ fī raddi al-jawābi
sentences.l: So he had the vizier Dandān brought, and said to him: Know that I have resolved upon a thing, so I mention (it) to you, and I want your being-informed of it; so be quick in the returning of the answer.
sentences.i: He summoned the vizier Dandān and said to him, “Know that I have made up my mind to something, and I will tell you of it, for I want you to know it; and be quick with your answer.”
sentences.n: fa-adhkuru laka, “so I will mention to you”, with no “it”: the object is left to be understood. iṭṭilāʿ ʿalā, “being made acquainted with”. radd al-jawāb, “returning the answer”, replying; the print marks the doubled dāl.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ مَاهُوَ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru dandānu mā huwa yā malika al-zamāni
sentences.l: And the vizier Dandān said: What is it, O king of the time?
sentences.i: “What is it, O king of the age?” asked the vizier Dandān.
sentences.n: The print runs mā huwa together (ماهو).

sentences.t: قَالَ عَزَمْتُ أَنْ أُسَلْطِنَ وَلَدِي كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَأَفْرَحَ بِهِ فِي حَيَاتِي وَأُقَاتِلَ قُدَّامَهُ إِلَى أَنْ يُدْرِكَنِى الْمَمَاتُ فَمَا عِنْدَكَ مِنَ الرَّأْىِ
sentences.tr: qāla ʿazamtu an usalṭina waladī kāna mā kāna wa-afraḥa bihi fī ḥayātī wa-uqātila quddāmahu ilā an yudrikanī al-mamātu fa-mā ʿindaka mina al-raʾyi
sentences.l: He said: I have resolved that I sultan my son Kān Mā Kān, and rejoice in him in my life, and fight before him until the death overtakes me. So what (is) with you of the opinion?
sentences.i: He said, “I have resolved to make my son Kān Mā Kān sultan, so that I may have the joy of him in my lifetime, and fight in front of him until death overtakes me. What is your advice?”
sentences.n: usalṭina, “make sultan”, the verb salṭana again. quddām, “in front of”, the spoken word for Classical amām. mā ʿindaka mina al-raʾy, “what have you of opinion?”: what do you advise? The print writes al-raʾy with its hamza (الرأى).

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ الْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ وَالسُّلْطَانُ صَاحِبُ الْعَصْرِ وَالْأَوَانِ أَنَّ مَاخَطَرَ بِبَالِكَ مَلِيحٌ غَيْرَ أَنَّهُ مَاهُوَ وَقْتُهُ الْآنَ لِخَصْلَتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbala al-wazīru dandānu al-arḍa bayna yadayi al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni wa-qāla lahu iʿlam ayyuhā al-maliku wa-al-sulṭānu ṣāḥibu al-ʿaṣri wa-al-awāni anna mā khaṭara bi-bālika malīḥun ghayra annahu mā huwa waqtuhu al-āna li-khaṣlatayni
sentences.l: And the vizier Dandān kissed the ground between the two hands of King Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and said to him: Know, O king and sultan, master of the age and the time, that what has occurred to your mind (is) fine; except that it, its time is not now, for two reasons.
sentences.i: The vizier Dandān kissed the ground before King Ḍawʾ al-Makān and said to him, “Know, O king and sultan, lord of this age and this time, that what has come into your mind is a fine thing; only, now is not the time for it, for two reasons.
sentences.n: ṣāḥib al-ʿaṣr wa-al-awān, “master of the age and the time”, a rhyming title of address. khaṭara bi-bālihi, “it occurred to his mind”. malīḥ, “fine, good”, in its spoken sense. mā huwa waqtuhu, “it is not its time”: mā with the pronoun huwa is the spoken negative. The print runs mā khaṭara and mā huwa together (ماخطر, ماهو), marks the doubled bāʾ of qabbala, and writes al-āna with its madda. khaṣla, “trait, point”: here “reason”.

sentences.t: الْأُولَى أَنَّ وَلَدَكَ كَانَ مَا كَانَ صَغِيرُ السِّنِّ
sentences.tr: al-ūlā anna waladaka kāna mā kāna ṣaghīru al-sinni
sentences.l: The first: that your son Kān Mā Kān (is) small of age.
sentences.i: The first is that your son Kān Mā Kān is still young;
sentences.n: ṣaghīr al-sinn, “small of tooth”: sinn, “tooth”, also means “age”, so “young in years”.

sentences.t: وَالثَّانِيَةُ مَا جَرَتْ بِهِ الْعَادَةُ أَنَّ مَنْ سَلْطَنَ وَلَدَهُ فِي حَيَاتِهِ لَا يَعِيشُ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا
sentences.tr: wa-al-thāniyatu mā jarat bihi al-ʿādatu anna man salṭana waladahu fī ḥayātihi lā yaʿīshu baʿda dhālika illā qalīlan
sentences.l: And the second (is) what the custom has run with: that whoever sultans his son in his life does not live after that except a little.
sentences.i: the second is what custom has always shown, that a man who makes his son sultan in his own lifetime does not live long after.
sentences.n: jarat bihi al-ʿāda, “custom has run with it”: it is the usual course of things. The print marks the doubled lām of illā (الّا).

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا مَا عِنْدِى مِنَ الْجَوَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā mā ʿindī mina al-jawābi
sentences.l: And this (is) what (is) with me of the answer.
sentences.i: That is the answer I have to give.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْوَزِيرُ أَنَّنَا نُوصِي عَلَيْهِ الْحَاجِبَ الْكَبِيرَ فَإِنَّهُ صَارَ مِنَّا وَإِلَيْنَا وَقَدْ تَزَوَّجَ أُخْتِي فَهُوَ فِي مَنْزِلَةِ أَخِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla iʿlam ayyuhā al-wazīru annanā nūṣī ʿalayhi al-ḥājiba al-kabīra fa-innahu ṣāra minnā wa-ilaynā wa-qad tazawwaja ukhtī fa-huwa fī manzilati akhī
sentences.l: And he said: Know, O vizier, that we will charge with him the Great Chamberlain, for he has become from us and to us, and he has married my sister, so he is in the station of my brother.
sentences.i: The king said, “Know, vizier, that we shall commend him to the care of the Great Chamberlain; for he has become one of us, and has married my sister, so that he stands to me as a brother.”
sentences.n: awṣā X ʿalā Y, “to charge X with the care of Y”: here the Great Chamberlain is given charge of the boy (ʿalayhi). minnā wa-ilaynā, “from us and to us”: one of our own. The print marks the doubled nūn of minnā and the doubled wāw of tazawwaja.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْوَزِيرُ افْعَلْ مَا بَدَالَكَ فَنَحْنُ مُطِيعُونَ أَمْرَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-wazīru ifʿal mā badā laka fa-naḥnu muṭīʿūna amraka
sentences.l: And the vizier said to him: Do what appears to you, for we (are) obeying your command.
sentences.i: The vizier said to him, “Do as you see fit; we are obedient to your command.”
sentences.n: The print runs badā laka together (بدالك). mā badā laka, “whatever seems good to you”. muṭīʿūna amraka: the participle takes its object directly, as the verb would.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلَ الْمَلِكُ إِلَى الْحَاجِبِ الْكَبِيرِ فَأَحْضَرَهُ وَكَذٰلِكَ أَكَابِرَ مَمْلَكَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-arsala al-maliku ilā al-ḥājibi al-kabīri fa-aḥḍarahu wa-ka-dhālika akābira mamlakatihi
sentences.l: And the king sent to the Great Chamberlain and had him brought, and likewise the great-ones of his kingdom.
sentences.i: So the king sent for the Great Chamberlain and had him brought, and the grandees of his kingdom as well.
sentences.n: akābir, plural of akbar, “the greatest”, are the grandees of the realm; here they are a second object of aḥḍara, “he had brought”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُمْ إِنَّ هٰذَا وَلَدِي كَانَ مَا كَانَ قَدْ عَلِمْتُمْ أَنَّهُ فَارِسُ أَهْلِ زَمَانِهِ وَلَيْسَ لَهُ نَظِيرٌ فِي حَرْبِهِ وَطِعَانِهِ وَقَدْ جَعَلْتُهُ سُلْطَانًا عَلَيْكُمْ وَالْحَاجِبُ الْكَبِيرُ عَمُّهُ وَهُوَ وَصِيٌّ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahum inna hādhā waladī kāna mā kāna qad ʿalimtum annahu fārisu ahli zamānihi wa-laysa lahu naẓīrun fī ḥarbihi wa-ṭiʿānihi wa-qad jaʿaltuhu sulṭānan ʿalaykum wa-al-ḥājibu al-kabīru ʿammuhu wa-huwa waṣiyyun ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And he said to them: This my son Kān Mā Kān, you have known that he is the horseman of the people of his time, and there is not for him an equal in his warring and his spear-thrusting; and I have made him sultan over you, and the Great Chamberlain is his uncle, and he is guardian over him.
sentences.i: And he said to them, “You know that this son of mine, Kān Mā Kān, is the finest horseman of his age, and has no equal in war and in the play of spears. I have made him sultan over you, and the Great Chamberlain, his uncle, is his guardian.”
sentences.n: Rhyming prose: zamānihi … ṭiʿānihi. ṭiʿān, “thrusting with spears, single combat”. The Chamberlain is ʿamm, “uncle”, loosely: he is the husband of the boy's aunt Nuzhat al-Zamān. waṣiyy ʿalā, “guardian over”, the one charged with a minor's affairs.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْحَاجِبُ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ مَا أَنَا إِلَّا غَرِيسُ نِعْمَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ḥājibu yā malika al-zamāni mā anā illā gharīsu niʿmatika
sentences.l: And the Chamberlain said: O king of the time, I am not but the planting of your favour.
sentences.i: The Chamberlain said, “O king of the age, I am nothing but a creature of your bounty.”
sentences.n: The print has غربس نعمنك, a misprint for غريس نعمتك, corrected here. gharīs, “something planted, a seedling”: what he is, the king's favour has planted and raised; the phrase is a courtly way of saying “I owe you everything” and so accepting the charge.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ ضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ أَيُّهَا الْحَاجِبُ إِنَّ وَلَدِي كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَابْنَةَ أَخِي قَضَيٰ فَكَانَ أَوْلَادُ عَمٍّ وَإِنِّي قَدْ زَوَّجْتُهَا بِهِ وَأَشْهَدَ الْحَاضِرِينَ عَلَى ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ḍawʾu al-makāni ayyuhā al-ḥājibu inna waladī kāna mā kāna wa-ibnata akhī qaḍā fakāna awlādu ʿammin wa-innī qad zawwajtuhā bihi wa-ashhada al-ḥāḍirīna ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān said: O Chamberlain, my son Kān Mā Kān and the daughter of my brother Qaḍā Fakān are children of an uncle, and I have married her to him. And he made the ones present witness to that.
sentences.i: Then Ḍawʾ al-Makān said, “Chamberlain, my son Kān Mā Kān and my brother's daughter Qaḍā Fakān are cousins, and I have given her to him in marriage.” And he called on all who were present to bear witness to it.
sentences.n: Qaḍā Fakān's name, and the dotted yāʾ the print gives it (قضي), were explained above. awlād ʿamm, “children of a paternal uncle”, i.e. cousins: the plural stands for two, as often in the spoken language, and marriage between such cousins was the favoured match. zawwaja … bi-, “to marry (her) to”: bi- marks the husband. The print marks the doubled wāw of zawwajtuhā. ashhada, “he made (them) witnesses”, takes the story out of his speech again.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَقَلَ لِوَلَدِهِ مِنَ الْمَالِ مَا يَعْجِزُ عَنْ وَصْفِهِ اللِّسَانُ
sentences.tr: thumma naqala li-waladihi mina al-māli mā yaʿjizu ʿan waṣfihi al-lisānu
sentences.l: Then he transferred to his son of the wealth what the tongue is powerless to describe.
sentences.i: Then he made over to his son more wealth than tongue can tell.
sentences.n: naqala li-, “to transfer to”: li- marks the one who receives. ʿajaza ʿan, “to be unable to (do)”.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ دَخَلَ عَلَى أُخْتِهِ نُزْهَةِ الزَّمَانِ وَأَعْلَمَهَا بِذٰلِكَ فَفَرِحَتْ وَقَالَتْ إِنَّ الِاثْنَيْنِ وَلَدَايَ أَبْقَاكَ اللّٰهُ وَتَعِيشُ لَهُمَا أَنْتَ مَدَى الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika dakhala ʿalā ukhtihi nuzhati al-zamāni wa-aʿlamahā bi-dhālika fa-fariḥat wa-qālat inna al-ithnayni waladāya abqāka allāhu wa-taʿīshu lahumā anta madā al-zamāni
sentences.l: And after that he went in to his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān and informed her of that; and she rejoiced and said: The two are my two children. May God keep you, and may you live for them, you, the length of time.
sentences.i: After that he went in to his sister Nuzhat al-Zamān and told her of it, and she was glad and said, “Both of them are my children. May God preserve you, and may you live for them to the end of time!”
sentences.n: aʿlama … bi-, “to inform of”: bi- marks the news. waladāya, “my two children”: she is aunt to both, and mother to neither. wa-taʿīshu, “and may you live”, an imperfect used as a wish, following on the prayer abqāka allāh, “may God keep you”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا أُخْتِي إِنِّي قَضَيْتُ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا مَا بِقَلْبِي وَأَمِنْتُ عَلَى وَلَدِي وَلٰكِنْ يَنْبَغِي أَنْ تُلَاحِظِيهِ بِعَيْنِكِ وَتُلَاحِظِي أُمَّهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā ukhtī innī qaḍaytu mina al-dunyā mā bi-qalbī wa-amintu ʿalā waladī wa-lākin yanbaghī an tulāḥiẓīhi bi-ʿayniki wa-tulāḥiẓī ummahu
sentences.l: And he said: O my sister, I have accomplished from the world what (was) in my heart, and I have become secure about my son; but it is fitting that you watch over him with your eye and watch over his mother.
sentences.i: He said, “Sister, I have had from this world all that my heart desired, and I am easy in my mind about my son; but you must keep an eye on him, and on his mother too.”
sentences.n: qaḍā min al-dunyā mā bi-qalbihi, “to fulfil from the world what is in one's heart”: to have had one's wish of life. amina ʿalā, “to feel safe about”. lāḥaẓa, “to watch over, keep an eye on”. The print marks the doubled mīm of ummahu.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَارَ يُوصِى الْحَاجِبَ وَنُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ عَلَى وَلَدِهِ وَبِنْتِ أَخِيهِ وَزَوْجَتِهِ لَيَالِيَ وَأَيَّامًا
sentences.tr: thumma ṣāra yūṣī al-ḥājiba wa-nuzhata al-zamāni ʿalā waladihi wa-binti akhīhi wa-zawjatihi layāliya wa-ayyāman
sentences.l: Then he began charging the Chamberlain and Nuzhat al-Zamān concerning his son and his brother's daughter and his wife, nights and days.
sentences.i: Then for days and nights together he kept commending his son, his niece and his wife to the care of the Chamberlain and Nuzhat al-Zamān.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “he began to, he went on”, a Middle Arabic habit. awṣā … ʿalā, “to enjoin (someone) to look after”: ʿalā marks those commended. The print spells yūṣī with a bare final yāʾ (يوصى).

sentences.t: وَقَدْ أَيْقَنَ بِكَأْسِ الْحِمَامِ وَلَزِمَ الْوِسَادَ وَصَارَ الْحَاجِبُ يَتَعَاطَيٰ أَحْكَامَ الْعِبَادِ وَالْبِلَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-qad ayqana bi-kaʾsi al-ḥimāmi wa-lazima al-wisāda wa-ṣāra al-ḥājibu yataʿāṭā aḥkāma al-ʿibādi wa-al-bilādi
sentences.l: And he had become certain of the cup of death, and kept to the pillow; and the Chamberlain began handling the governance of the servants (of God) and the lands.
sentences.i: He was now sure that he must drink the cup of death, and he kept to his bed; and the Chamberlain took in hand the government of the people and the land.
sentences.n: ayqana bi-, “to be certain of”: the verb takes bi-. kaʾs al-ḥimām, “the cup of death”, a stock figure; ḥimām is fate, the appointed death. lazima al-wisād, “to cling to the pillow”, to be bedridden. taʿāṭā, “to take in hand, to undertake”; the print writes it with a dotted yāʾ (يتعاطي). al-ʿibād wa-al-bilād, “the servants (of God) and the lands”, a rhyming pair for subjects and realm.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ سَنَةٍ أَحْضَرَ وَلَدَهُ كَانَ مَاكَانَ وَالْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ وَقَالَ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ هٰذَا الْوَزِيرَ وَالِدُكَ مِنْ بَعْدِى
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda sanatin aḥḍara waladahu kāna mā kāna wa-al-wazīra dandāna wa-qāla yā waladī inna hādhā al-wazīra wāliduka min baʿdī
sentences.l: And after a year he had his son Kān Mā Kān brought, and the vizier Dandān, and said: O my son, this vizier is your father after me.
sentences.i: A year later he sent for his son Kān Mā Kān and for the vizier Dandān, and said, “My son, after I am gone this vizier is your father.
sentences.n: The print runs mā kāna together here (ماكان). It writes baʿdī with a bare final yāʾ (بعدى).

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنِّي رَاحِلٌ مِنَ الدَّارِ الْفَانِيَةِ إِلَى الدَّارِ الْبَاقِيَةِ وَقَدْ قَضَيْتُ غَرَضِي مِنَ الدُّنْيَا وَلٰكِنْ بَقِيَ فِي قَلْبِي حَسْرَةٌ يُزِيلُهَا اللّٰهُ عَلَى يَدَيْكَ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam annī rāḥilun mina al-dāri al-fāniyati ilā al-dāri al-bāqiyati wa-qad qaḍaytu gharaḍī mina al-dunyā wa-lākin baqiya fī qalbī ḥasratun yuzīluhā allāhu ʿalā yadayka
sentences.l: And know that I am departing from the abode, the passing one, to the abode, the remaining one; and I have accomplished my aim from the world, but there remains in my heart a regret which God will remove at your two hands.
sentences.i: Know that I am leaving this passing world for the world that endures. I have had what I wanted of this life; but one grief remains in my heart, and God will take it away by your hand.”
sentences.n: al-dār al-fāniya, “the perishing abode”, this world, against al-dār al-bāqiya, “the lasting abode”, the next. ḥasra, “sorrow, bitter regret”. ʿalā yadayka, “at your hands”, by your agency. baqiya, masculine, before the feminine ḥasra: the verb often stays masculine when it comes first and something stands between.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَلَدُهُ وَمَا تِلْكَ الْحَسْرَةُ يَا وَالِدِى
sentences.tr: fa-qāla waladuhu wa-mā tilka al-ḥasratu yā wālidī
sentences.l: And his son said: And what is that regret, O my father?
sentences.i: “And what is that grief, father?” asked his son.
sentences.n: The print writes wālidī with a bare final yāʾ (والدى).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا وَلَدِى أَنْ أَمُوتَ وَلَمْ آخُذْ بِثَأْرِ جَدِّكَ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ وَعَمِّكَ الْمَلِكِ شَرْكَانَ مِنْ عَجُوزٍ يُقَالُ لَهَا ذَاتُ الدَّوَاهِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā waladī an amūta wa-lam ākhudh bi-thaʾri jaddika ʿumara bni al-nuʿmāni wa-ʿammika al-maliki sharrukāna min ʿajūzin yuqālu lahā dhātu al-dawāhī
sentences.l: And he said: O my son, that I die and have not taken the blood-revenge of your grandfather ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān and your uncle King Sharrukān from an old woman who is called Dhāt al-Dawāhī.
sentences.i: He said, “My son, it is that I die without having avenged your grandfather ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān and your uncle King Sharrukān on an old woman called Dhāt al-Dawāhī.
sentences.n: an amūta, “that I should die”, answers the question: the grief is this. akhadha bi-thaʾri X min Y, “to take X's blood-revenge on Y”: bi- marks the vengeance, min the one it is taken from. The print writes thaʾr without its hamza (ثار), but puts the madda on ākhudh (آخذ); it marks the doubled mīm of ʿammika.

sentences.t: فَإِنْ أَعْطَاكَ اللّٰهُ النَّصْرَ لَا تَنَمْ عَنْ أَخْذِ الثَّأْرِ وَكَشْفِ الْعَارِ مِنَ الْكُفَّارِ وَإِيَّاكَ مِنْ مَكْرِ الْعَجُوزِ وَاقْبَلْ مَا يَقُولُهُ لَكَ الْوَزِيرُ دَنْدَانُ لِأَنَّهُ عِمَادُ مُلْكِنَا مِنْ قَدِيمِ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-in aʿṭāka allāhu al-naṣra lā tanam ʿan akhdhi al-thaʾri wa-kashfi al-ʿāri mina al-kuffāri wa-iyyāka min makri al-ʿajūzi wa-iqbal mā yaqūluhu laka al-wazīru dandānu li-annahu ʿimādu mulkinā min qadīmi al-zamāni
sentences.l: So if God gives you victory, do not sleep from the taking of the revenge and the uncovering of the shame from the unbelievers; and beware you of the cunning of the old woman; and accept what the vizier Dandān says to you, because he is the pillar of our kingship from old of time.
sentences.i: If God grants you victory, do not rest until you have taken vengeance and wiped away our shame at the hands of the unbelievers. Beware of the old woman's cunning, and take the advice the vizier Dandān gives you, for he has been the pillar of our kingdom since days of old.”
sentences.n: Rhyming prose: al-thaʾr … al-ʿār … al-kuffār. nāma ʿan, “to sleep on, to neglect”. kashf al-ʿār, “removing the disgrace”. iyyāka min, “beware of”, a looser construction than Classical iyyāka wa-. The sukūn on iqbal (واقبلْ) is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَبِلَ مِنْهُ وَلَدُهُ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qabila minhu waladuhu dhālika
sentences.l: And his son accepted that from him.
sentences.i: His son took this charge from him.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ هَمَلَتْ عَيْنَاهُ بِالدُّمُوعِ وَازْدَادَ بِهِ الْمَرَضُ
sentences.tr: thumma hamalat ʿaynāhu bi-al-dumūʿi wa-izdāda bihi al-maraḍu
sentences.l: Then his two eyes poured with tears, and the sickness increased upon him.
sentences.i: Then the king's eyes ran with tears, and his sickness grew worse.
sentences.n: hamalat, “flowed, streamed”: bi- marks what they pour. ʿaynāhu are the father's eyes. izdāda bihi, “grew upon him”: bi- here is “in him, with him”.

sentences.t: وَصَارَ أَمْرُ الْمَمْلَكَةِ لِلْحَاجِبِ صِهْرِهِ وَكَانَ رَجُلًا كَبِيرًا فَصَارَ يَحْكُمُ وَيَأْمُرُ وَيَنْهَى وَاسْتَمَرَّ عَلَى ذٰلِكَ سَنَةً كَامِلَةً
sentences.tr: wa-ṣāra amru al-mamlakati li-al-ḥājibi ṣihrihi wa-kāna rajulan kabīran fa-ṣāra yaḥkumu wa-yaʾmuru wa-yanhā wa-istamarra ʿalā dhālika sanatan kāmilatan
sentences.l: And the affair of the kingdom came to the Chamberlain, his in-law, and he was a big man; and he began to rule and command and forbid, and continued upon that a whole year.
sentences.i: So the rule of the kingdom passed to the Chamberlain, his brother-in-law, who was a man of years; and he governed, giving orders and forbidding, and went on so for a full year.
sentences.n: ṣihr, “relative by marriage”: the Chamberlain is married to the king's sister. rajul kabīr, “a big man”, most likely “an elderly man”, though it may mean “a man of rank”. yaʾmuru wa-yanhā, “he commands and forbids”, the stock phrase for wielding authority; the print itself has the hamza in yaʾmuru (يأمر).

sentences.t: وَضَوْءُ الْمَكَانِ مَشْغُولٌ بِمَرَضِهِ وَلَمْ تَزَلْ تُنْهِكُهُ الْأَمْرَاضُ إِلَى أَرْبَعِ سِنِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-ḍawʾu al-makāni mashghūlun bi-maraḍihi wa-lam tazal tunhikuhu al-amrāḍu ilā arbaʿi sinīna
sentences.l: And Ḍawʾ al-Makān was occupied with his sickness, and the sicknesses did not cease wearing him down up to four years.
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān, meanwhile, was taken up with his illness, and his ailments went on wasting him for four years.
sentences.n: mashghūl bi-, “busy with”: bi- marks what occupies him. anhaka, “to exhaust, wear out”. ilā arbaʿi sinīn, “up to four years”, i.e. for as long as four years.

sentences.t: وَقَعَدَ الْحَاجِبُ الْكَبِيرُ بِالْمُلْكِ وَارْتَضَى بِهِ أَهْلُ الْمَمْلَكَةِ وَأَكَابِرُ الدَّوْلَةِ وَدَعَتْ لَهُ جَمِيعُ الْبِلَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-qaʿada al-ḥājibu al-kabīru bi-al-mulki wa-irtaḍā bihi ahlu al-mamlakati wa-akābiru al-dawlati wa-daʿat lahu jamīʿu al-bilādi
sentences.l: And the Great Chamberlain sat with the kingship, and the people of the kingdom and the great-ones of the state were content with him, and all the lands prayed for him.
sentences.i: The Great Chamberlain held the throne, the people of the kingdom and the grandees of the state were well content with him, and in every land prayers were said for him.
sentences.n: qaʿada bi-al-mulk, “to sit with the kingship”, to take charge of the realm; the vocalisation mulk, “rule”, rather than milk or malik, is ours. irtaḍā bi-, “to be content with, accept”. daʿā li-, “to pray for”: to be named in the Friday prayers was the public sign of a ruler.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ وَالْحَاجِبِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri ḍawʾi al-makāni wa-al-ḥājibi
sentences.l: This is what was of the affair of Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the Chamberlain.
sentences.i: So much for Ḍawʾ al-Makān and the Chamberlain.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the tale and taking up another; the print runs mā kāna together.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ ابْنِ الْمَلِكِ كَانَ مَاكَانَ فَلَيْسَ لَهُ شُغْلٌ إِلَّا رُكُوبَ الْخَيْلِ وَاللَّعِبَ بِالرُّمْحِ وَالضَّرْبَ بِالنُّشَّابِ وَكَذٰلِكَ بِنْتُ عَمِّهِ قَضَى فَكَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri ibni al-maliki kāna mā kāna fa-laysa lahu shughlun illā rukūba al-khayli wa-al-laʿiba bi-al-rumḥi wa-al-ḍarba bi-al-nushshābi wa-ka-dhālika bintu ʿammihi qaḍā fakāna
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of the king's son Kān Mā Kān, there was not for him any occupation except the riding of horses and playing with the lance and shooting with arrows, and likewise his uncle's daughter Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.i: As for the king's son Kān Mā Kān, he had no other business than riding horses, sporting with the lance and shooting with the bow; and so too his cousin Qaḍā Fakān.
sentences.n: The print puts a shadda on illā (الّا). laʿiba bi-al-rumḥ, “to play with the lance”, mock combat on horseback. al-ḍarb bi-al-nushshāb, “striking with arrows”, i.e. archery; nushshāb is a collective, “arrows”. laysa, present in form, stands here in a past narrative. The girl shares her cousin's sports: she is to be a warrior too.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تَخْرُجُ هِيَ وَإِيَّاهُ مِنْ أَوَّلِ النَّهَارِ إِلَى اللَّيْلِ فَتَدْخُلُ هِيَ إِلَى أُمِّهَا وَيَدْخُلُ هُوَ إِلَى أُمِّهِ فَيَجِدُهَا جَالِسَةً عِنْدَ رَأْسِ أَبِيهِ تَبْكِي فَيَخْدُمُهُ بِاللَّيْلِ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat takhruju hiya wa-iyyāhu min awwali al-nahāri ilā al-layli fa-tadkhulu hiya ilā ummihā wa-yadkhulu huwa ilā ummihi fa-yajiduhā jālisatan ʿinda raʾsi abīhi tabkī fa-yakhdumuhu bi-al-layli ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: And she used to go out, she and him, from the first of the day to the night; then she would go in to her mother and he would go in to his mother, and he would find her sitting at the head of his father, weeping, and he would serve him by night until the morning.
sentences.i: She and he would ride out together from the start of the day till nightfall. Then she would go in to her mother and he to his, and he would find his mother sitting at his father's bedside, weeping; and he would wait on his father through the night until morning.
sentences.n: hiya wa-iyyāhu, “she and him”: the spoken language joins the object pronoun iyyāhu where Classical Arabic wants huwa. The sentence turns on its pronouns: the mother (-hā) sits weeping, the son serves the father (-hu).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ يَخْرُجُ هُوَ وَبِنْتُ عَمِّهِ عَلَى عَادَتِهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma yakhruju huwa wa-bintu ʿammihi ʿalā ʿādatihimā
sentences.l: Then he would go out, he and his uncle's daughter, according to their custom.
sentences.i: Then he and his cousin would go out again as they always did.
sentences.n: ʿalā ʿādatihimā, “according to the custom of the two of them”: ʿalā here is “in keeping with”.

sentences.t: وَطَالَتْ بِضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ التَّوَجُّعَاتُ فَبَكَى وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-ṭālat bi-ḍawʾi al-makāni al-tawajjuʿātu fa-bakā wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And the pains grew long with Ḍawʾ al-Makān, and he wept and recited, saying these verses:
sentences.i: Ḍawʾ al-Makān's sufferings dragged on, and he wept and recited these verses:
sentences.n: ṭāla bi-, “to last long for (someone)”: bi- marks the sufferer. tawajjuʿāt, “aches, sufferings”, plural of tawajjuʿ, “feeling pain, complaining of pain”.

sentences.t:
تَفَانى قُوَّتِيْ وَمَضىٰ زَمَانِيْ * وَهَا اَنَا قَدْ بَقِيْتُ كَمَا تَرَانِيْ
فَيَوْمَ الْعِزِّ كُنْتُ اَعَزَّ قَوْمِيْ * وَاَسْبَقَهُمْ اِلى نَيْلِ الْاَمَانِيْ
تَرَى قَبْلَ الْمَمَاتِ اَرَى لِوُلْدِيْ * يَكُوْنُ عَلَى الْوَرَى مَلِكُ مَكَانِيْ
وَيَفْتِكُ بِالْعِدَاةِ لِاَخْذِ ثَارِ * بِضَرْبِ السَّيْفِ اَوْ طَعْنِ السَّنَانِ
اَنَا الْمَغْبُوْنُ فِيْ هَزْلٍ وَجِدٍّ * اِذَا مَوْلَايَ لَا يَشْفِيْ جِنَانِيْ
sentences.tr:
tafānā quwwatī wa-maḍā zamānī * wa-hā anā qad baqītu kamā tarānī
fa-yawma al-ʿizzi kuntu aʿazza qawmī * wa-asbaqahum ilā nayli al-amānī
tarā qabla al-mamāti arā li-wuldī * yakūnu ʿalā al-warā maliku makānī
wa-yaftiku bi-al-ʿidāti li-akhdhi thāri * bi-ḍarbi al-sayfi aw ṭaʿni al-sinānī
anā al-maghbūnu fī hazlin wa-jiddin * idhā mawlāya lā yashfī janānī
sentences.l:
My strength has wasted away and my time has passed, * and here I am, I have remained as you see me.
And on the day of might I was the mightiest of my people, * and the swiftest of them to the attaining of the hopes.
Do-you-think, before death, I shall see for my child * (that) there is over mankind a king (in) my place,
and he falls-upon the enemies to take revenge * with the striking of the sword or the thrusting of the spearhead?
I am the cheated one in jest and in earnest * if my Lord does not heal my heart.
sentences.i:
My strength is spent, my day is done, * and here I lie, as you see me now.
In the days of my glory I was first of my people * and swiftest of them all to win what I hoped for.
Shall I live, before I die, to see my son * set up as king over men in my place,
falling upon the enemy to take revenge * with the stroke of the sword and the thrust of the spear?
I am the loser, in sport and in earnest, * if my Lord will not heal my heart.
sentences.n: Five lines in the metre wāfir, all rhyming in -ānī, copied as the print points them. tafānā, “to waste away utterly”. tarā, literally “do you see?”, opens a wondering question: “I wonder, shall I see …?”. wuld, “child”, a by-form of walad. The print points maliku with a single ḍamma, as the subject of yakūnu, “that there should be over mankind a king in my place”, with makānī standing loosely for “in my place”; the sense is that his son should reign after him. thāri is thaʾr, “blood-revenge”, without its hamza, as in the prose above. al-maghbūn, “the one cheated in a bargain”: his life will have been a bad bargain. janān, “heart, the inmost self”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغَ مِنْ شِعْرِهِ وَضَعَ رَأْسَهُ عَلَى الْوِسَادَةِ فَغَفَلَتْ عَيْنُهُ فَنَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faragha min shiʿrihi waḍaʿa raʾsahu ʿalā al-wisādati fa-ghafalat ʿaynuhu fa-nāma
sentences.l: And when he had finished from his poetry, he put his head on the pillow, and his eye grew-heedless, and he slept.
sentences.i: When he had finished his verses he laid his head on the pillow; his eyes grew heavy, and he slept.
sentences.n: ghafalat ʿaynuhu, “his eye became heedless”: he dozed off.

sentences.t: فَرَأَى فِي مَنَامِهِ قَائِلًا يَقُولُ لَهُ أَبْشِرْ فَإِنَّ وَلَدَكَ يَمْلَأُ الْبِلَادَ عَدْلًا وَيَمْلِكُهَا وَتُطِيعُهُ الْعِبَادُ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾā fī manāmihi qāʾilan yaqūlu lahu abshir fa-inna waladaka yamlaʾu al-bilāda ʿadlan wa-yamlikuhā wa-tuṭīʿuhu al-ʿibādu
sentences.l: And he saw in his sleep a sayer saying to him: Receive-good-tidings, for your son will fill the lands (with) justice and will possess them, and the servants (of God) will obey him.
sentences.i: And in his sleep he saw someone who said to him, “Rejoice! Your son will fill the lands with justice and rule them, and all people will obey him.”
sentences.n: abshir, “rejoice at good news”, from bushrā, “glad tidings”. ʿadlan, “with justice”: an accusative of specification after yamlaʾu, “to fill”. al-ʿibād, “the servants (of God)”, mankind. The rhyme falls on al-bilāda … al-ʿibādu. The print points yamlaʾu itself.

sentences.t: فَانْتَبَهَ مِنْ مَنَامِهِ مَسْرُورًا مِنْ هٰذِهِ الْبِشَارَةِ الَّتِي رَآهَا
sentences.tr: fa-intabaha min manāmihi masrūran min hādhihi al-bishārati allatī raʾāhā
sentences.l: And he woke from his sleep glad from this good-tidings which he had seen.
sentences.i: He woke from his sleep gladdened by the good news he had seen in his dream.
sentences.n: bishāra, “good tidings”, from the same root as abshir.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ بَعْدَ أَيَّامٍ قَلَائِلَ طَرَقَهُ الْمَمَاتُ فَأَصَابَ أَهْلَ بَغْدَادَ لِمَوْتِهِ غَمٌّ عَظِيمٌ وَبَكَى عَلَيْهِ الْوَضِيعُ وَالْعَظِيمُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu baʿda ayyāmin qalāʾila ṭaraqahu al-mamātu fa-aṣāba ahla baghdāda li-mawtihi ghammun ʿaẓīmun wa-bakā ʿalayhi al-waḍīʿu wa-al-ʿaẓīmu
sentences.l: Then, after few days, the death knocked-at him; and there struck the people of Baghdad at his death a great grief, and there wept over him the lowly and the great.
sentences.i: Then, a few days later, death came knocking for him. The people of Baghdad were struck with great grief at his death, and high and low wept for him.
sentences.n: ṭaraqahu, “it knocked at his door by night, it came upon him”. qalāʾil, “few”, a plural of qalīl. li-mawtihi, “because of his death”: li- gives the cause. A rhyme closes the sentence: ʿaẓīmun … wa-al-ʿaẓīmu.

sentences.t: وَمَضَى عَلَيْهِ الزَّمَانُ كَأَنَّهُ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-maḍā ʿalayhi al-zamānu ka-annahu mā kāna
sentences.l: And the time passed over him as-though he was not.
sentences.i: And time passed over him as though he had never been.
sentences.n: ka-annahu mā kāna, “as if he had not been”: the same words, mā kāna, as in his son's name Kān Mā Kān, “What was, was”, which follows at once. The print marks the doubled nūn of ka-annahu.

sentences.t: وَتَغَيَّرَ حَالُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ وَعَزَلَهُ أَهْلُ بَغْدَادَ وَجَعَلُوهُ هُوَ وَعِيَالَهُ فِي مَكَانٍ عَلَى حِدَتِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-taghayyara ḥālu kāna mā kāna wa-ʿazalahu ahlu baghdāda wa-jaʿalūhu huwa wa-ʿiyālahu fī makānin ʿalā ḥidatihim
sentences.l: And the state of Kān Mā Kān changed, and the people of Baghdad set-him-aside and put him, him and his household, in a place apart-by-themselves.
sentences.i: And Kān Mā Kān's fortunes changed: the people of Baghdad passed him over and lodged him and his household in a place apart.
sentences.n: ʿazala, “to remove, depose, set aside”: the boy is passed over for the throne. ʿiyāl, “household, dependants”. ʿalā ḥidatihim, “on their own, separately”, from ḥida, “being alone” (root w-ḥ-d). The print marks the doubled yāʾ of taghayyara.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْ أُمُّ كَانَ مَا كَانَ ذٰلِكَ صَارَتْ فِي أَذَلِّ الْأَحْوَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾat ummu kāna mā kāna dhālika ṣārat fī adhalli al-aḥwāli
sentences.l: And when the mother of Kān Mā Kān saw that, she came-to-be in the most-abject of the states.
sentences.i: When Kān Mā Kān's mother saw this, she was brought to the lowest of conditions.
sentences.n: ṣārat fī, “she came to be in”. adhall, “most abject”, elative of dhalīl, “lowly, humbled”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَابُدَّ لِي مِنْ قَصْدِ الْحَاجِبِ الْكَبِيرِ وَأَرْجُو الرَّأْفَةَ مِنَ اللَّطِيفِ الْخَبِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lā budda lī min qaṣdi al-ḥājibi al-kabīri wa-arjū al-raʾfata mina al-laṭīfi al-khabīri
sentences.l: And she said: There is no escape for me from going-to the Great Chamberlain, and I hope (for) the compassion from the Kind, the All-Aware.
sentences.i: And she said, “I have no choice but to go to the Great Chamberlain, and I look for compassion from Him who is Kind and All-Aware.”
sentences.n: lā budda li … min, “there is no way out for … from, I must”; the print runs lā budda together (لابد). al-Laṭīf al-Khabīr, “the Subtly Kind, the All-Aware”, two of the names of God, paired in the Qurʾān. The rhyme falls on al-kabīri … al-khabīri.

sentences.t: فَقَامَتْ مِنْ مَنْزِلِهَا إِلَى أَنْ أَتَتْ إِلَى بَيْتِ الْحَاجِبِ الَّذِى صَارَ سُلْطَانًا فَوَجَدَتْهُ جَالِسًا عَلَى فِرَاشِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāmat min manzilihā ilā an atat ilā bayti al-ḥājibi alladhī ṣāra sulṭānan fa-wajadathu jālisan ʿalā firāshihi
sentences.l: And she rose from her dwelling until she came to the house of the Chamberlain who had become sultan, and found him sitting on his couch.
sentences.i: She set out from her lodging and went to the house of the Chamberlain, who was now sultan, and found him sitting on his couch.
sentences.n: ilā an, “until”. firāsh, literally “bed, spread”, here the cushioned seat on which a ruler sits.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَتْ عِنْدَ زَوْجَتِهِ نُزْهَهِ الزَّمَانِ وَبَكَتْ بُكَاءً شَدِيدًا وَقَالَتْ لَهَا إِنَّ الْمَيِّتَ مَا لَهُ صَاحِبٌ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalat ʿinda zawjatihi nuzhati al-zamāni wa-bakat bukāʾan shadīdan wa-qālat lahā inna al-mayyita mā lahu ṣāḥibun
sentences.l: And she went-in to-by his wife Nuzhat al-Zamān, and wept a violent weeping, and said to her: The dead (man) has no friend.
sentences.i: She went in to his wife, Nuzhat al-Zamān, wept bitterly, and said to her, “The dead have no friends.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿinda, “to go in to (someone)”, is the spoken idiom for dakhala ʿalā. Nuzhat is printed here with hāʾ for tāʾ marbūṭa (نزهه). mā lahu ṣāḥibun, “he has no companion”: once a man is dead no one stands by his own. The direct speech runs on through the next three sentences.

sentences.t: فَلَا أَحْوَجَكُمُ اللّٰهُ مَدَى الدُّهُورِ وَالْأَعْوَامِ وَلَا زِلْتُمْ تَحْكُمُونَ بِالْعَدْلِ بَيْنَ الْخَاصِّ وَالْعَامِّ
sentences.tr: fa-lā aḥwajakumu allāhu madā al-duhūri wa-al-aʿwāmi wa-lā ziltum taḥkumūna bi-al-ʿadli bayna al-khāṣṣi wa-al-ʿāmmi
sentences.l: So may God not make-you-needy for the length of the ages and the years, and may you not cease ruling with justice between the elite and the common.
sentences.i: May God never bring you to need, through all the ages and the years, and may you ever judge with justice between the great and the common folk!
sentences.n: lā with a past verb is a wish: lā aḥwajakumu allāhu, “may God not make you needy”; lā ziltum, “may you not cease”. The plural “you” is respectful, and takes in her husband. al-khāṣṣ wa-al-ʿāmm, “the select and the common”: everyone. The rhyme falls on al-aʿwāmi … al-ʿāmmi.

sentences.t: قَدْ سَمِعَتْ أُذُنَاكِ وَرَأَتْ عَيْنَاكِ مَا كُنَّا فِيهِ مِنَ الْمُلْكِ وَالْعِزِّ وَالْجَاهِ وَالْمَالِ وَحُسْنِ الْمَعِيشَةِ وَالْحَالِ
sentences.tr: qad samiʿat udhunāki wa-raʾat ʿaynāki mā kunnā fīhi mina al-mulki wa-al-ʿizzi wa-al-jāhi wa-al-māli wa-ḥusni al-maʿīshati wa-al-ḥāli
sentences.l: Your two ears have heard and your two eyes have seen what we were in of the kingship and the glory and the rank and the wealth and the goodness of the living and the state.
sentences.i: Your own ears have heard and your own eyes have seen in what royalty, honour, standing and wealth we lived, in what ease of life and fortune.
sentences.n: udhunāki, ʿaynāki, “your two ears, your two eyes”: duals, feminine “you”. jāh, “rank, standing, influence”. The print marks the doubled zāy of al-ʿizz. The rhyme falls on al-māli … al-ḥāli.

sentences.t: وَالْآنَ انْقَلَبَ عَلَيْنَا الزَّمَانُ وَخَانَنَا الدَّهْرُ وَالْأَوَانُ وَقَصَدَنَا بِالْعُدْوَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-al-āna inqalaba ʿalaynā al-zamānu wa-khānanā al-dahru wa-al-awānu wa-qaṣadanā bi-al-ʿudwāni
sentences.l: And now the time has turned against us, and the age and the season have betrayed us and made-for us with the enmity.
sentences.i: And now time has turned against us; fate and fortune have betrayed us and set upon us with hostility.
sentences.n: inqalaba ʿalā, “to turn over against”. qaṣada … bi-, “to make for (someone) with”: bi- marks what it comes with. The print itself points qaṣadanā. Three rhymes in a row: al-zamānu … al-awānu … al-ʿudwāni.

sentences.t: وَأَتَيْتُ إِلَيْكِ قَاصِدَةً إِحْسَانَكِ بَعْدَ إِسْدَائِي لِلْإِحْسَانِ لِأَنَّهُ إِذَا مَاتَ الرَّجُلُ ذَلَّتْ بَعْدَهُ النِّسَاءُ وَالْبَنَاتُ
sentences.tr: wa-ataytu ilayki qāṣidatan iḥsānaki baʿda isdāʾī li-al-iḥsāni li-annahu idhā māta al-rajulu dhallat baʿdahu al-nisāʾu wa-al-banātu
sentences.l: And I have come to you seeking your kindness, after my bestowing of the kindness; because, when the man dies, the women and the daughters are humbled after him.
sentences.i: I have come to you seeking your kindness, I who once was the giver of kindness; for when a man dies, the women and daughters he leaves behind are brought low.”
sentences.n: isdāʾ, verbal noun of asdā, “to do (a favour), to bestow”: li- marks its object, al-iḥsān. The rhyme falls on iḥsānaki … li-al-iḥsāni. The print marks the doubled lām of dhallat.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَتْ تَقُولُ هٰذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ شِعْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma anshadat taqūlu hādhihi al-abyāta shiʿrun
sentences.l: Then she recited, saying these verses — poetry:
sentences.i: Then she recited these verses:

sentences.t:
كَفَاكَ بِاَنَّ الْمَوْتَ بَادِي الْعَجَائِبِ * وَمَا غَائِبُ الْاَعْمَارِ عَنَّا بِغَائِبِ
وَمَا هٰذِهِ الْاَيَّامُ اِلَّا مَرَاحِلُ * مَوَارِدُهَا مَمْزُوجَةٌ بِالْمَصَائِبِ
وَمَا ضَرَّ قَلْبِي مِثْلُ فَقْدِ اَكَارِمٍ * اَحَاطَتْ بِهِمْ مُسْتَعْظَمَاتُ النَّوَائِبِ
sentences.tr:
kafāka bi-anna al-mawta bādī al-ʿajāʾibi * wa-mā ghāʾibu al-aʿmāri ʿannā bi-ghāʾibi
wa-mā hādhihi al-ayyāmu illā marāḥilu * mawāriduhā mamzūjatun bi-al-maṣāʾibi
wa-mā ḍarra qalbī mithlu faqdi akārimin * aḥāṭat bihim mustaʿẓamātu al-nawāʾibi
sentences.l:
It suffices you that the death (is) manifest of the wonders, * and the absent (part) of the lifetimes is not absent from us.
And these days are not but stages, * their watering-places mixed with the calamities.
And nothing harmed my heart like the loss of noble-ones * whom the enormities of the disasters surrounded.
sentences.i:
Let this be lesson enough: death's wonders are plain to see; * the end of our lives, though hidden, is never far away.
These days of ours are nothing but stages on a road, * and every halting-place has its waters mixed with grief.
Nothing has wounded my heart like the loss of noble men * whom the heaviest blows of misfortune hemmed about.
sentences.n: kafāka bi-, “it is enough for you that”: bi- marks what suffices. bādī al-ʿajāʾib, “plain in its wonders”. ghāʾib al-aʿmār, “what is hidden of lifetimes”, the unknown hour of death; the bi- of bi-ghāʾibi only strengthens the negative. marāḥil, “stages of a journey”, the day's marches between halts; mawārid, “watering-places” on the way. mustaʿẓamāt al-nawāʾib, “the calamities that are counted grievous”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ نُزْهَةُ الزَّمَانِ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ تَذَكَّرَتْ أَخَاهَا ضَوْءَ الْمَكَانِ وَابْنَهُ كَانَ مَا كَانَ فَقَرَّبَتْهَا وَأَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat nuzhatu al-zamāni hādhā al-kalāma tadhakkarat akhāhā ḍawʾa al-makāni wa-ibnahu kāna mā kāna fa-qarrabathā wa-aqbalat ʿalayhā
sentences.l: And when Nuzhat al-Zamān heard this speech, she remembered her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his son Kān Mā Kān, and she drew-her-near and turned-towards her.
sentences.i: When Nuzhat al-Zamān heard these words she remembered her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān and his son Kān Mā Kān; she drew the woman close and received her warmly.
sentences.n: aqbala ʿalā again: here, to greet her kindly. The print marks the doubled kāf of tadhakkarat and the doubled rāʾ of qarrabathā.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ أَنَا الْآنَ وَاللّٰهِ غَنِيَّةٌ وَأَنْتِ فَقِيرَةٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat anā al-āna wa-allāhi ghaniyyatun wa-anti faqīratun
sentences.l: And she said: I now, by God, (am) rich, and you (are) poor.
sentences.i: And she said, “Now, by God, I am rich and you are poor.

sentences.t: فَوَاللّٰهِ مَا تَرَكْنَا افْتِقَادَكِ إِلَّاخَوْفًا مِنِ انْكِسَارِ قَلْبِكِ لِئَلَّا يَخْطُرَ بِبَالِكِ أَنَّ مَا نُهْدِيهِ إِلَيْكِ صَدَقَةٌ مَعَ أَنَّ جَمِيعَ مَا نَحْنُ فِيهِ مِنَ الْخَيْرِ مِنْكِ وَمِنْ زَوْجِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-wa-allāhi mā taraknā iftiqādaki illā khawfan mini inkisāri qalbiki li-allā yakhṭura bi-bāliki anna mā nuhdīhi ilayki ṣadaqatun maʿa anna jamīʿa mā naḥnu fīhi mina al-khayri minki wa-min zawjiki
sentences.l: And by God, we did not leave-off seeking-you-out except (from) fear of the breaking of your heart, lest it occur to your mind that what we give to you (is) alms; though all that we are in of the good (is) from you and from your husband.
sentences.i: By God, we stayed away from visiting you only for fear of wounding your pride, lest you should think that what we sent you was charity, when all the good we enjoy has come from you and your husband.
sentences.n: iftiqād, “seeking out, looking in on (someone)”, to see how they fare. inkisār al-qalb, “the breaking of the heart”: humiliation. khaṭara bi-bālihi, “to cross his mind”: bi- is “in”. ṣadaqa, “alms, charity”. The print runs illā khawfan together as one word (الاخوفا).

sentences.t: فَبَيْتُنَا بَيْتُكِ وَمَحَلُّنَا مَحَلُّكِ وَلَكِ مَالَنَا وَعَلَيْكِ مَا عَلَيْنَا
sentences.tr: fa-baytunā baytuki wa-maḥallunā maḥalluki wa-laki mā lanā wa-ʿalayki mā ʿalaynā
sentences.l: So our house (is) your house, and our place (is) your place, and to you (is) what (is) to us, and upon you what (is) upon us.
sentences.i: Our house is your house and our home your home: what is ours is yours, and what we owe, you share.”
sentences.n: laki mā lanā wa-ʿalayki mā ʿalaynā, “yours is what is ours, and on you is what is on us”: a set phrase for full and equal partnership, in both rights and duties. The print runs mā lanā together (مالنا); it could also be read mālunā, “our wealth”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَلَعَتْ عَلَيْهَا ثِيَابًا فَاخِرَةً وَأَفْرَدَتْ لَهَا مَكَانًا فِى الْقَصْرِ مُلَاصِقًا لِمَكَانِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma khalaʿat ʿalayhā thiyāban fākhiratan wa-afradat lahā makānan fī al-qaṣri mulāṣiqan li-makānihā
sentences.l: Then she robed her (in) splendid clothes, and set-apart for her a place in the palace adjoining her (own) place.
sentences.i: Then she dressed her in splendid robes of honour and gave her quarters of her own in the palace, next to her own rooms.
sentences.n: khalaʿa ʿalā, “to bestow a robe of honour on”, as in units 71 and 90. afrada li-, “to set apart for”.

sentences.t: وَأَقَامَتْ عِنْدَهُمْ فِي عِيشَةٍ طَيِّبَةٍ هِيَ وَوَلَدُهَا كَانَ مَا كَانَ
sentences.tr: wa-aqāmat ʿindahum fī ʿīshatin ṭayyibatin hiya wa-waladuhā kāna mā kāna
sentences.l: And she stayed with them in a good living, she and her son Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.i: And she lived with them in comfort, she and her son Kān Mā Kān.
sentences.n: ʿīsha, “manner of life”.

sentences.t: وَأَلْبَسَتْهُ ثِيَابَ الْمُلُوكِ وَأَفْرَدَتْ لَهُمَا الْجَوَارِيَ بِرَسْمِ خِدْمَتِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-albasathu thiyāba al-mulūki wa-afradat lahumā al-jawāriya bi-rasmi khidmatihimā
sentences.l: And she clothed him (in) the clothes of the kings, and set-apart for the two of them the slave-girls by-way-of serving-them.
sentences.i: She dressed the boy in kingly clothes and assigned slave-girls to wait on the two of them.
sentences.n: bi-rasmi, “for (the service of)”, as in unit 95. The subject is Nuzhat al-Zamān.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ بَعْدَ مُدَّةٍ قَلِيلَةٍ ذَكَرَتْ لِزَوْجِهَا حَدِيثَ زَوْجَةِ أَخِيهَا ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna nuzhata al-zamāni baʿda muddatin qalīlatin dhakarat li-zawjihā ḥadītha zawjati akhīhā ḍawʾi al-makāni
sentences.l: Then Nuzhat al-Zamān, after a little while, told to her husband the story of the wife of her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān.
sentences.i: A little while later Nuzhat al-Zamān told her husband about her brother Ḍawʾ al-Makān's wife.

sentences.t: فَدَمَعَتْ عَيْنَاهُ وَقَالَ إِنْ شِئْتِ أَنْ تَنْظُرِي الدُّنْيَا بَعْدَكِ فَانْظُرِيهَا بَعْدَ غَيْرِكِ فَأَكْرِمِي مَثْوَاهَا
sentences.tr: fa-damaʿat ʿaynāhu wa-qāla in shiʾti an tanẓurī al-dunyā baʿdaki fa-unẓurīhā baʿda ghayriki fa-akrimī mathwāhā
sentences.l: And his two eyes shed-tears, and he said: If you wish to see the world after you, then see it after other-than-you; so honour her lodging.
sentences.i: His eyes filled with tears, and he said, “If you would know how the world will be after you are gone, look at how it is after others are gone. Make her welcome, and treat her with honour.”
sentences.n: The saying means: how the world treats the family of another when he is dead shows how it will treat yours. akrimī mathwāhā, “make her stay honourable”, echoes the Qurʾān (12:21), where the Egyptian who has bought Joseph says to his wife akrimī mathwāhu.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
